entries.Detail (verified fact, in our words): Surgeons usually refer patients to the Vanderbilt Preoperative Evaluation Center (VPEC) before surgery. The visit is free and checks overall surgical risk. VPEC has two locations: The Vanderbilt Clinic (TVC) and One Hundred Oaks (OHO). Nurse practitioners see patients in person; registered nurses do phone visits. Staff check vital signs, take images, screen for sleep apnea, and review history and systems. Lab work and X-rays can be done at the visit or through a local primary care doctor for phone-visit patients.
entries.Flag / verify note: This page is written for staff; the facts are consistent with the patient-facing anesthesiology page.

entries.Detail (verified fact, in our words): VPEC evaluates patients before surgery at Vanderbilt University Hospital and its satellite surgery centers, working with surgeons to decide what tests are needed. Visits can be in person or by phone.

Vanderbilt tells patients to understand the instructions for the night before and morning of surgery, including eating, drinking and bathing. The specific rules are NOT published online — they come from the surgeon's office or VPEC.
Vanderbilt advises confirming with your doctor's office where you will be admitted and what time to arrive. Arrival time and exact check-in desk for surgery are not published online.

The surgical waiting area is on level 2 of the renovated Vanderbilt University Hospital lobby (renovation completed February 2023). Medical admitting is on the first floor. A large digital display board was installed on each lobby floor.

entries.Detail (verified fact, in our words): The renovated lobby has extra wall and floor power outlets, furniture with built-in charging ports, a work bar with power ports on each floor, and smaller alcoves where families can sit together.
Check in with the Guest Services representative when you arrive in the surgical waiting area. Guest Services keeps families updated on the surgery's progress.

entries.Topic: Visitors on the day of surgery
entries.Detail (verified fact, in our words): Hospital-wide rule: up to 2 visitors in a patient's room 9 a.m.–9 p.m. To prevent crowding in waiting areas, visitors swapping places should do so outside the hospital.
entries.Flag / verify note: No separate surgery-day visitor rule is published for the main hospital.

entries.Detail (verified fact, in our words): Masks are optional for most people; some patients with respiratory symptoms will be asked to wear one. Do not visit if you have symptoms of illness. Wash hands or use sanitizer entering and leaving patient rooms.
2 visitors may be in a patient's room, including ICUs, 9 a.m.–9 p.m. One of the two may be a child of any age with an adult 18+ (see ICU exception).
For children 10 and under visiting an ICU (other than trauma), contact the unit charge nurse before the visit. For trauma units, call the unit first; age limits vary.

1 adult (18+) may stay in the room after 9 p.m. and overnight. No overnight visitors in semi-private rooms. Vanderbilt tries to give every patient a private room but may use semi-private rooms when appropriate.

If the care team determines a patient is nearing end of life, the number of visitors is decided with the unit manager, administrative coordinator and family. At least one visitor must be 18+ if children visit.
The Neuro ICU (unit 6T3) is on the 6th floor of the Critical Care Tower (CCT), which sits between The Vanderbilt Clinic (TVC) and Vanderbilt University Hospital (VUH).
23 ICU beds and 12 step-down beds.
Brain tumors, strokes, spinal cord injury, neuromuscular disorders, and other diseases of the brain, nerves and spinal cord. A specialized critical care team is on site 24/7.

On arrival at the 6th floor, check in with the Guest Services representative at the Information Desk. After hours, buzz in near the main ICU entrance to reach the Medical Receptionist. Staff will help you find the room, show you resources, explain how to get a visitation PASS, and answer questions.
The 6th-floor atrium is a quiet, sunlit room with plenty of seating, suited for larger families.

No one may enter the Neuro ICU without an ID tag or Visitation PASS. Get a PASS at the 6T3 waiting room information desk or the Medical Receptionist desk just inside the ICU before going to the room. When you switch with another family member or leave the unit, leave your PASS with the Medical Receptionist or in the basket; reclaim it when you return. Do not stand or gather in the hallway (it violates other patients' privacy).
2 visitors per room. Daytime PASSES show the number 1 or 2 and the patient's ICU room number.

entries.Detail (verified fact, in our words): Several teams care for each patient: Neurology, Neurosurgery, Critical Care, consult services (e.g., epilepsy, palliative care, cardiology, kidney), nursing, and respiratory/occupational/physical/speech therapy. Plans can change within minutes as new labs, imaging or exam results come in. All teams talk with each other. Families are encouraged to ask any team any question; if a team can't answer, it will find the team that can. Nursing and critical care teams are always present in the ICU.
Brain-surgery discharge instructions and warning signs are NOT published online. Ask the neurosurgery team for written instructions and an after-hours number.
